newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: U.S. says intends to continue aid to Palestinians.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says intends to continue aid to Palestinians.

text.p: The United States wants to continue aid to the Palestinians despite concerns over their adherence to commitments to work to control violence against Israel, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Monday.
"We'd like to continue assistance to the Palestinians. That has been the basis of our policy since 1993" when Israel and the Palestinians signed the Oslo peace accord, he told reporters.
Burns, accompanying Secretary of State Madeleine Albright to a Southeast Asia regional meeting, could not explain how the aid might be continued.

The U.S. law that makes it possible for the United States to have official dealings with and give aid to Yasser Arafat's Palestinian Authority is to expire on August 12 and there is doubt about whether Congress will extend the law before it leaves for its August recess.

Expiration of the Middle East Peace Facilitation Act would cut off U.S. financial assistance to the Palestinians, terminate diplomatic contacts and force the Palestinian Liberation Office to close its Washington office.

Moreover, the Washington Post reported that even if the law was extended, aid and contacts might have to be cut off at least for a while because the administration could not issue the required certification that the Palestinians were complying with their obligations under the Oslo peace agreements.
Ending aid to the Palestinians would be another major blow to the embattled Middle East peace process.

The United States has provided $260 million out of a five-year commitment of $500 million to the Palestinians and "we think in the interest of peace we need to continue assistance to the Palestinian people," Burns said.
He stressed that most if not all of the U.S. funds go to non-governmental organisations who work with the Palestinian people, not to the Palestinian Authority.

Anti-Palestinian sentiment has been rising in Congress over the past six months as negotiations between Israel and the Palestinians over implementing their agreement have broken down and violence has flared in the occupied territories.
Burns could not explain how the administration could certify that Palestinians were complying with their Oslo obligations.

But he noted Arafat had said he would prosecute four Palestinian police officers arrested recently by Israeli police for apparently plotting a terrorist strike against Israel and called that "positive."
